section.title: The Birth of Jesus
section.sectionRationale: Having established Jesus' royal line, Matthew now tells how this child entered the world: not by the ordinary course of the genealogy but by the Holy Spirit, born of a virgin. The scene turns on Joseph, a righteous man wrestling with a crisis, and on an angel's word that unveils who this child is and what He has come to do.
section.thesis: The child conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary is Jesus, the one who saves His people from their sins, and Immanuel, God with us, so that in His birth the promises of God and the very presence of God come to dwell among His people.
section.frameNote: Four beats: Mary's pregnancy and Joseph's dilemma; the angel's revelation of the child's name and mission; the fulfillment of Isaiah's prophecy of Immanuel; and Joseph's quiet obedience.

verses.text: This is how the birth of Jesus Christ came about: His mother Mary was pledged in marriage to Joseph, but before they came together, she was found to be with child through the Holy Spirit.
Because Joseph her husband was a {{dikaios|righteous}} man and was unwilling to disgrace her publicly, he resolved to divorce her quietly.

units.label: The angel's word
units.note: you are to give Him the name Jesus

verses.text: But after he had pondered these things, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream and said, “Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to embrace Mary as your wife, for the One conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.
She will give birth to a Son, and you are to give Him the name {{iesous|Jesus}}, because He will save His people from their sins.”

units.label: To fulfill what was spoken
units.note: the virgin will be with child

verses.text: All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had said through the prophet:
“Behold, the {{parthenos|virgin}} will be with child and will give birth to a son, and they will call Him {{emmanouel|Immanuel}}” (which means, “God with us”).

units.label: Joseph obeys
units.note: he did as the angel commanded

verses.text: When Joseph woke up, he did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him and embraced Mary as his wife.
But he had no union with her until she gave birth to a Son. And he gave Him the name Jesus.

dikaios.gloss: Righteous, just, upright. Joseph's righteousness is shown not in rigid punishment but in a desire to obey God while sparing Mary shame; his character sets the tone for the obedient, tender-hearted man God entrusts with His Son.

iesous.gloss: Jesus, the Greek form of the Hebrew Yeshua or Joshua, meaning the LORD saves. The name is a job description: He will save His people from their sins. The angel ties the name directly to the mission of rescue that the whole Gospel unfolds.

parthenos.gloss: Virgin, a young unmarried woman who has not known a man. Matthew cites the Greek of Isaiah 7:14, where parthenos renders the Hebrew almah; the conception by the Holy Spirit fulfills the sign, so that this child has no human father.

emmanouel.gloss: Immanuel, Hebrew for God with us. Matthew makes it the frame of his whole Gospel: the child is God present with His people at the start, and at the end the risen Jesus promises, I am with you always, to the end of the age.

basic.context: Mary and Joseph were pledged in marriage, a binding commitment stronger than a modern engagement, when Mary was found to be pregnant. Joseph, knowing the child was not his, faced an agonizing choice. As a righteous man he planned to end the marriage quietly, to spare Mary public shame, until an angel revealed the truth in a dream and told him the child's name and mission.
basic.hermeneutics: This is history told to reveal who Jesus is. Matthew centers the account on Joseph rather than Mary, because his aim is to show that Jesus is legally David's heir and truly God with us. The angel's explanation of the name Jesus, and the quotation of Isaiah, are the interpretive keys: they tell us not just what happened but what it means.
basic.originalLanguages: The name Jesus means the LORD saves, and the angel spells out why: He will save His people from their sins. The prophecy speaks of a virgin, a woman who has not known a man, and names the child Immanuel, God with us. These two names, Jesus and Immanuel, sum up the whole Gospel: God has come, and God has come to save.
basic.typology: Isaiah's sign of Immanuel, given in a moment of national crisis, finds its deepest meaning here. The presence of God that filled the tabernacle and temple now takes on flesh in a child. The greater Joshua has come to lead His people, not into a land, but out of the deeper bondage of sin.
basic.christ: This passage is entirely about Christ: conceived by the Spirit, born of a virgin, named Jesus because He saves, and called Immanuel because He is God with us. He is fully human, born of Mary, and truly divine, God dwelling among us. His mission is named before His birth: to save His people from their sins.
basic.god: God enters His own world. The Holy Spirit conceives the child; the Father sends the angel; the Son is God with us. God does not save from a distance but comes near, taking flesh, to rescue a people who could never rescue themselves. And He works through the quiet obedience of an ordinary righteous man.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 7:14 is the prophecy quoted, the virgin and Immanuel. Luke 1 tells the annunciation to Mary. Philippians 2 describes the Son taking human form. And Matthew 28:20 closes the Gospel with the risen Jesus promising to be with us always, echoing Immanuel.
basic.oneStory: The God who has been keeping His promises through the long genealogy now steps personally into the story. In a manger lies both the answer to Israel's hope and the presence of God Himself. His name tells us the whole plot: He has come to save His people from their sins, and He will be with them to the very end.

context.literary:
The paragraph is built around a single hinge, the dream of verse 20, with trouble on one side and obedience on the other. Verses 18 and 19 set out a problem and a private resolve. Verses 20 to 23 give the angel's speech, which contains three things in a deliberate order: a command ('do not be afraid to embrace Mary'), a reason ('the One conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit'), and a mission ('you are to give Him the name Jesus'). Verses 24 and 25 then show Joseph carrying out each instruction, so the paragraph ends with the problem solved by obedience.

The passage is told from Joseph's side, and it is told with striking restraint. Mary does not speak, and no scene of the conception is described. Verse 18 says only that she was 'found to be with child through the Holy Spirit,' and the narrator tells the reader the cause before Joseph knows it. We therefore read verse 19 with knowledge Joseph does not have, which makes his gentleness more moving.

The unit also carries the first of Matthew's quotations introduced by the formula 'to fulfill what the Lord had said through the prophet.' The word 'fulfill' will return again and again through the Gospel, and its first use is here, in the verse that explains the name. Matthew himself translates the Hebrew name for his Greek readers, 'God with us,' as the evangelist pauses his narrative to translate.

There is also a quiet inclusion with the end of the Gospel. The name Immanuel at 1:23 and the promise 'I am with you always' at 28:20 stand at either end of the book, and the first sentence about the child's name is balanced by the last sentence about His presence. Verse 25 closes with the naming, the very act the angel commanded, so the paragraph begins with the question of who the father is and ends with the father giving the name.
context.historical:
Marriage in the Jewish world of the first century had two stages. The betrothal was a legally binding covenant, sealed in the presence of witnesses and carrying the legal weight of marriage, so that a betrothed man was already called 'husband,' as Matthew does in verse 19. It was followed some months later by the bringing of the bride into the husband's house, and only then did the couple 'come together.' Ending the betrothal required a formal divorce. A betrothed woman found with child by someone other than her husband was liable to serious penalty, and the law of Deuteronomy 22:23-24 shows that the sexual unfaithfulness of a betrothed woman was treated with the gravity of adultery. Matthew gives no indication that Joseph would have pressed for the harshest penalty, and he describes only the option he chose.

The law also allowed a husband to write a certificate of divorce and hand it to his wife, Deuteronomy 24:1, so a quiet ending without a public hearing was open to him. Joseph chooses that course, and the choice, more than any word, shows his character.

The naming of a child was the father's task and also his acceptance of the child as his own. Joseph's obedience in naming the baby, verse 25, therefore has legal as well as spiritual significance: it places Jesus within David's house. The angel addresses him as 'Joseph, son of David,' a title that reminds him of whose line he belongs to and what is at stake.

The theme of dreams would also have been familiar. Revelation by dream appears in the story of the patriarch Joseph, Genesis 37:5, and Matthew will give Joseph three more dreams in the next chapter, including one that sends the family to Egypt, Matthew 2:13, and one that brings them back, Matthew 2:19-20. A reader who knew the Old Testament would hear in the name Joseph and the pattern of dreams an echo of the Joseph who saved a family in Egypt.
context.canonical:
Two Old Testament passages sit behind this paragraph, and one is quoted outright. The first is Isaiah 7:14, from the days of King Ahaz, when the house of David was shaken by the threat of Aram and Israel, 'the hearts of Ahaz and his people trembled like trees in the forest shaken by the wind,' Isaiah 7:2. Isaiah told him not to fear and offered a sign. Ahaz refused, and the prophet gave one anyway: 'Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel.' The name returns twice more in Isaiah 8, in verses 8 and 10, where 'God is with us' becomes a defiance of the nations, and Isaiah 9:6-7 speaks of a child born to reign on David's throne for ever. Matthew sees the child of Isaiah 7 and the king of Isaiah 9 meeting in Jesus.

The second is the promise to David, 2 Samuel 7:12-16, which Joseph's title 'son of David' and the naming of the child in David's house bring back. The earlier genealogy has traced the line to Joseph, and this paragraph shows how Jesus enters it.

The name Jesus is the Greek form of Joshua, and its meaning is spelled out for the reader: 'He will save His people from their sins.' That line is close to Psalm 130:8, 'He will redeem Israel from all iniquity.' The theme of God dwelling with His people runs from Exodus 29:45-46, where He says, 'I will dwell among the Israelites,' through Leviticus 26:12, 'I will walk among you,' and Ezekiel 37:27 to John 1:14, 'The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us.'

The New Testament also treats the conception as a doctrine. Luke tells the other side of the story: Mary's question 'How can this be, since I am a virgin?' and the angel's reply that the Holy Spirit will come upon her, Luke 1:34-35. Paul says that God sent His Son 'born of a woman,' Galatians 4:4, and the creed language that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary has Matthew 1 and Luke 1 as its roots. The paragraph is therefore one of the foundations of the church's confession about who Jesus is.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew wanted his readers to understand where Jesus came from, and he does not allow the question to hang. The child is not the product of a hidden scandal, and Joseph is not a deceived man. Every move in the story is designed to answer an unspoken charge. Any such pregnancy invites suspicion, and Matthew meets it by telling the whole story from the inside, with Joseph's own agony and the angel's word.

He also meant them to see the child's identity and mission as one. The name Jesus means 'the LORD saves,' and the angel gives the reason at once: He will save His people from their sins. The title Immanuel adds the other half, that God is with them. A hearer who has taken in both names knows that the One in Mary's womb is the very presence of God and the saving act of God at once, and he knows what the child is for before He has done anything.

Finally, Matthew wanted to show what faithful response looks like. Joseph is a model of a righteous man who is brought by revelation to a costly obedience. He does not demand explanations; he wakes up and does 'as the angel of the Lord had commanded him.' Matthew's readers, who were being asked to trust a crucified Messiah, were meant to see themselves in a man who believed the word of God when it asked something hard.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage records a unique event and does not describe a pattern. The conception of Jesus by the Holy Spirit is not repeated, and nowhere is anyone told to expect or seek such a birth. It is the signature of the one Savior, not a template for the family. In the same way, a dream that changes the course of a man's life is something that happened to Joseph, and the passage does not tell readers to wait for dreams. The Bible's instruction for guidance is elsewhere in the written word.

Joseph's own conduct is another matter. The text commends him by calling him righteous, and it records his actions without comment, yet the way Matthew tells the story invites us to learn from it. His restraint in the face of what looked like betrayal, his refusal to retaliate, and his willingness to obey when obedience cost him his reputation are held up as admirable. They are not laws for every situation, but they show the kind of character the Lord uses. What clearly carries forward is doctrine: that Jesus is God with us and the Savior from sin, a truth to believe and to build a life upon.

debates.question: Does Isaiah 7:14 speak of a virgin, and how is it fulfilled in Jesus?

views.label: A true virgin conception fulfilling the prophecy fully in Christ
views.case: Matthew cites the Greek of Isaiah, which reads parthenos, virgin, and presents the conception by the Spirit as the complete, intended fulfillment; the sign of Immanuel finds its true depth only in the child who is actually God with us.

views.label: A near-term sign in Isaiah's day with ultimate fulfillment in Jesus
views.case: Isaiah's word had an initial reference to a child born in his own time as a sign to Ahaz, yet Matthew, guided by the Spirit, sees its fullest and final meaning in the virgin-born Christ.

debates.bearing: Either way Matthew reads Jesus as the true Immanuel; the New Testament rests the incarnation on this text, and the virgin birth safeguards both His full humanity and His deity.

debates.question: In what sense was Joseph righteous in wanting to divorce Mary quietly?

views.label: Righteousness expressed as merciful restraint
views.case: Joseph honored the law's seriousness about apparent unfaithfulness yet refused to expose Mary to public shame, showing a righteousness that longs to do right while tempering justice with compassion.

views.label: Righteousness as reverent reluctance before a holy mystery
views.case: On this reading Joseph suspected something of God at work and, unwilling to presume, sought to step aside quietly; his righteousness is a humble hesitance before what he did not yet understand.

debates.bearing: Both portraits commend a righteousness that is neither harsh nor lax, and both are answered by the angel, who tells Joseph the truth and calls him to take Mary as his wife.

debates.question: What does 'no union with her until she gave birth' say about Mary afterward?

views.label: Mary remained a virgin all her life
views.case: The church's older tradition, held in the Orthodox and Catholic churches and by some Reformers, reads the clause as saying what happened before the birth and nothing about after. They argue that the Greek word for 'until' does not by itself imply a change and that the 'brothers' of Jesus are Joseph's children by an earlier marriage or relatives.

views.label: Mary and Joseph had a normal marriage afterward
views.case: Many Protestants read the natural sense as implying that normal marital relations began after the birth, and take the brothers and sisters of Matthew 13:55-56 as Jesus' younger siblings.

views.label: The text is not trying to settle it
views.case: A third approach holds that Matthew's only concern is to protect the virginal conception before the birth. The 'until' clause makes that point and stops, and later questions are answered on other grounds.

debates.bearing: The passage is guarding the origin of Jesus and does not set out to answer later questions. What every view must keep is the virginal conception before the birth, which is what the text asserts.

study.originalLanguages:
The language of the paragraph carries more than the English reveals, and it is worth looking at a few words closely. In verse 18 Mary was 'pledged in marriage,' a passive participle that names the first stage of Jewish marriage. The same stage is why Joseph is called her 'husband' in verse 19, though they had not come together. Matthew says she was 'found,' a verb that suggests discovery by others, and he adds the explanation 'through the Holy Spirit' before Joseph knows, a phrase that returns in the angel's words in verse 20. In both places the Greek preposition is the one used for origin, 'out of,' so the conception is traced to the Spirit as its source.

In verse 19 the adjective dikaios, 'righteous,' is paired with a participle meaning 'not willing,' and then comes a rare verb, deigmatisai, which means to expose to public disgrace. Paul uses a related form when he says Christ made a 'public spectacle' of the powers at the cross, Colossians 2:15. The contrast is sharp. Joseph will not make a public example of Mary, and he plans instead to 'put her away,' the ordinary word for divorce, 'quietly,' that is, in secret. Matthew also uses the word 'pondered' in verse 20, a participle that suggests turning a matter over in the mind, and it tells us that Joseph's decision was not impulsive.

The command in verse 20 is 'do not be afraid to take Mary,' using the verb paralambano, to take alongside, which is what Joseph does in verse 24. Matthew thus lets the angel's word and Joseph's action match exactly.

In verse 21 the angel says 'you are to give Him the name Jesus,' which is literally 'you will call His name Jesus,' a future form that functions as a command. The Greek Iesous is the form of the Hebrew Yeshua, Joshua, 'the LORD saves,' and Moses had given this name to Hoshea, Numbers 13:16. The explanation 'because He will save' uses the emphatic pronoun autos, 'He Himself will save,' which marks the saving as His own work and not a delegated one. The object is 'His people,' the people of the covenant, and the thing saved from is 'their sins,' not their enemies. That is a surprise for a nation looking for rescue from Rome.

Verse 23 quotes Isaiah with the word parthenos for 'virgin.' The Hebrew of Isaiah 7:14 has the word almah, a young woman of marriageable age, used for Rebekah in Genesis 24:43, and that same Rebekah is described as a virgin by another word in Genesis 24:16. The Greek translators of Isaiah rendered the word parthenos, and Matthew follows that rendering. Matthew himself gives the translation of the name Immanuel, 'God with us,' using the Greek verb for translating.

In the last verse the imperfect tense in 'he had no union with her' means that he was not knowing her, a continuing state, and it is followed by a phrase that means 'until the point at which,' which sets the limit of the statement at the birth.

typology.type: Immanuel, the sign of God's presence
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah gave the name Immanuel to a child as a sign to King Ahaz that God was with the house of David in a time of fear, Isaiah 7:14 and 8:8-10. The tabernacle and temple were the earlier signs of God dwelling among His people, Exodus 29:45-46 and Exodus 40:34-35. In Jesus, Matthew says, the sign becomes a person. John says that the Word 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, and Jesus tells the disciples, 'where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them,' Matthew 18:20. The escalation is from a sign about God to God Himself in flesh. The type falls short because earlier signs could point to God's nearness, but only the incarnation could close the distance.

The angel gives the child the name Jesus, the same name as Joshua, who led Israel across the Jordan and into the land, Numbers 13:16. Joshua saved a people from enemies and gave them rest. Hebrews says that if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day, Hebrews 4:8. The escalation in Jesus is that the enemy is sin and the rest is God's own, and His rescue is complete: 'He will save His people from their sins.' The correspondence falls short because Joshua's conquest could not remove sin from the hearts of the conquered, and Joshua himself died.

typology.type: Ahaz and Joseph, sons of David who are told not to fear
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah's scene and Matthew's are alike. In Isaiah, the house of David is afraid and its king is told 'Do not be afraid,' Isaiah 7:4, and the sign is offered; Ahaz refuses. In Matthew a son of David is told 'do not be afraid,' and he receives the sign and obeys. The contrast between the faithless king and the faithful carpenter shows that the promise to David does not depend on the throne's occupant. The escalation is that the sign Ahaz refused is carried into history by a man with no crown. The type falls short because Joseph is not the child's father, and the child, not Joseph, is the one who will reign.

typology.type: Sons born by the power of God, from Isaac to Jesus
typology.fulfillment: Scripture tells of births that God Himself made possible: Isaac to the aged Sarah, 'the LORD did for Sarah what He had promised,' Genesis 21:1-2, and later Samuel and John. Each shows that the line of promise depends on God and not on human power. Jesus' birth intensifies the pattern. Where Isaac was born to a father and mother beyond the age of children, Jesus is conceived with no human father, and Mary is told, 'no word from God will ever fail,' Luke 1:37. The pattern falls short because every earlier child had two human parents, and none of them was God with us.

study.christ:
The paragraph is wholly about Christ, and the question is how it leads to Him rather than whether. It does so first by His names. 'Jesus' is the name Moses gave to Hoshea, Joshua, 'the LORD saves,' and the angel makes the meaning plain: He Himself will save His people from their sins. The Old Testament had said that God would redeem Israel from all iniquity, Psalm 130:8, and that was a promise nobody could keep apart from God. To call the child by a name meaning 'the LORD saves' is to say that in Him the LORD does what He promised. Peter says, 'Salvation exists in no one else,' Acts 4:12.

It leads to Christ by the title Immanuel. In Isaiah the name expressed the hope of God's presence. Matthew says the name is true of the child in a literal way, and John states the same thing at greater length: the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. That is how Matthew's Gospel ends too, with the risen Jesus saying, 'I am with you always,' Matthew 28:20. He is the one whose presence is the content of the whole book.

It leads to Christ by His two origins. 'Conceived by the Holy Spirit' and 'born of Mary' stand together. He is fully human, since He is born of a woman, Galatians 4:4, and He is fully divine, since His conception is from the Spirit and His name is God with us. Paul says God sent 'His own Son in the likeness of sinful man, as an offering for sin,' Romans 8:3, and Hebrews says that He shared our flesh and blood, Hebrews 2:14. The virgin birth does not make Him less human; it ensures that the human who stands in our place is also the God who saves.

It leads to Christ through Joseph. By taking Mary as wife and naming the child, Joseph brings Jesus into David's house. The genealogy in the earlier paragraph ends with Joseph the husband of Mary, and this paragraph shows how the line still reaches the child. The adoptive naming makes Jesus heir of David's promise while the conception from the Spirit makes Him more than David's son. Later He will ask the Pharisees how the Christ can be David's son and David's Lord, Matthew 22:41-45, and the answer is already here.

The mission of the child is also named before He does anything: He will save from sins. That is the verdict on His whole life, from the manger to the cross, where He says 'This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins,' Matthew 26:28. The first chapter has already told us what the last will accomplish.

A caution is in order. Not every detail of the narrative is a symbol of Jesus. Joseph's dream and his silence are history, not code. The links above rest on the New Testament's own use of Isaiah, the names, and the doctrine of the incarnation.
study.god:
The paragraph shows a God who comes close and who works in secret before He works in public. The conception takes place in a small home in Galilee with no witness but Mary, and the first public mention of it is a problem in a village. God does not announce Himself with a display; He enters the world in a way that looks, to everyone who does not know, like a scandal. His humility is part of His character. The God of the covenant does not avoid the possibility of being misjudged.

It shows a Trinitarian shape. The Holy Spirit is the agent of the conception, the Lord who sends His angel is the God of Israel, and the child is the one called Immanuel, God with us. Matthew does not state a doctrine of the Trinity, but the three persons are each at work in a single sentence, and the church's later reflection grew from texts like this one.

It shows that God is faithful to a word He spoke centuries earlier. The sign that Isaiah gave to a frightened king was not forgotten, and it was brought to its fullest sense when the time was right. Paul says, 'when the time had fully come, God sent His Son,' Galatians 4:4. The angel's own comment is, 'no word from God will ever fail,' Luke 1:37, and the quotation from Isaiah in the paragraph shows that to be true.

It shows a God who saves by coming. The name Jesus and the title Immanuel together mean that He does not rescue from a distance and does not send a deputy. Salvation is accomplished by the presence of God in flesh, which is the point of the incarnation. The Son who is 'from the Holy Spirit' is the one who will 'save His people from their sins,' so the Savior and the God are one.

It shows a God who treats human beings with dignity. He sends an angel to Joseph, explains the situation, and trusts him to act. Joseph is not a pawn; he is told the truth and asked for obedience. The same God who could simply have arranged the facts stops to reassure a frightened man, and speaks first the words 'do not be afraid.'

For worship, the paragraph invites wonder and gratitude. It is the right place to hear the song of Christmas, that the Lord of all came near in weakness. It also invites trust in the God who asks hard obedience, because the one who asks is also the one who is with us. The believer can say with Joseph's household that the God who gave the command also provided the presence, and the child who was named by the angel is named again by every Christian who calls on the name of Jesus.

crossReferences.note: The context of the prophecy Matthew quotes. King Ahaz is offered a sign and refuses to ask, and Isaiah gives one anyway to the whole house of David. Reading the whole scene shows that the sign is first of all about God's faithfulness to David's line, which is why it fits Joseph, a son of David.

The name Immanuel returns here, first as a cry to the land being overrun, 'O Immanuel,' then as a defiance of the nations: 'For God is with us.' The name carries both comfort and challenge, and Matthew's use of it carries both as well.

A child is born and a son given, with the government on His shoulders, and He will reign on David's throne for ever. The royal child of this prophecy and the sign child of chapter 7 are, for Matthew, one person.

The LORD does for Sarah what He had promised and she bears Isaac in old age. It is the first of the Bible's births by the power of God, and it shows the pattern that the birth of Jesus both continues and surpasses.

Luke tells the same event from Mary's side. She asks how it can be since she is a virgin, and the angel says the Holy Spirit will come upon her and that no word from God will fail. Read with Matthew, it gives the full picture of both parents.

The psalm ends with the promise that the LORD will redeem Israel from all iniquity. The angel's words to Joseph, that the child will save His people from their sins, carry this promise to the point of its fulfillment.
The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. John's sentence is the long form of Matthew's 'Immanuel,' and its word for dwelling recalls the tabernacle where God lived among His people.

God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law, when the time had fully come. Paul states in a line the doctrine that Matthew narrates, that the Son has a real human birth and that it happens at the moment God has chosen.

God sent His own Son in the likeness of sinful man as an offering for sin. It connects the birth with the purpose in the angel's word: He is born in order to deal with sin, the thing He is named to save from.

The Son, in the form of God, took the form of a servant and was made in human likeness. The hymn follows the downward movement of the incarnation that Matthew begins at Bethlehem, and it ends in the cross.

The risen Jesus promises to be with His disciples always, to the end of the age. It stands at the other end of the Gospel from 'God with us,' and shows that Immanuel is not a title for the nativity but the character of His whole ministry.
Joseph's next dream commands him to take the child and flee to Egypt. It shows that the obedience of 1:24 was the first of several, and that his faith was tested again at once.

study.oneStory:
The paragraph is the point where the Old Testament's two great hopes, a king and God's own presence, come together in one child. From Genesis onward, the Bible's story is a story of presence lost and presence promised. In Eden God walked with His creatures, Genesis 3:8, and was driven out of their lives by sin. He promised a seed. At Sinai He promised to dwell among His people, and the tabernacle and the temple were the sign, but the glory departed in the days of exile. Isaiah's sign to Ahaz was given in the darkest days of the kingdom, and its name, God with us, has been the quiet hope of the faithful ever since.

Matthew shows how that hope is met. The Holy Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation, Genesis 1:2, now overshadows a young woman in Nazareth. The seed of the woman is born. The son of David is given his name. The name that meant 'the LORD saves' in Joshua's day now belongs to the child who will save from the thing that made the exile in the first place, sin. The temple that was emptied of glory is replaced by a body in which God dwells.

It sets up the shape of the rest of the Gospel. The infants of Bethlehem will be threatened, the family will flee to Egypt and return as Israel did, and the child will be baptized, tempted and sent. The opposition that rises in Matthew 2 shows that the promised king arrives in a world that is hostile to Him, and the ending will show that the hostility is overcome. The angel's promise that He will save is proved at the cross and in the resurrection, and His promise to be with us is renewed in the last verse.

It also sets up the church's confession. The creeds say 'conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary' because this paragraph and Luke's say it. Without a real conception from the Spirit there would be no one who is both God and man, and without that union there would be no Savior who could die for human beings and also have the power to forgive. The virgin birth is therefore a hinge in the story of salvation, not a decoration on a legend.

It ends in the new creation. In Revelation the voice from the throne says, 'Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them. They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God,' Revelation 21:3. The presence that was a sign in Isaiah's day and a baby in Joseph's house becomes the permanent reality of a renewed earth. Immanuel is not only a name for the manger. It is the last word of the Bible's story.

quiz.q: How was Mary found to be with child?

options.text: Through the Holy Spirit, before she and Joseph came together.
options.note: Verse 18 states plainly that the conception was through the Holy Spirit.

options.text: By a miracle of God, in a way Joseph could not explain.
options.note: True in effect, but the text names the Holy Spirit specifically as the agent of conception.

options.text: After she and Joseph were fully married and living together.
options.note: The text says it was before they came together, during betrothal.

options.text: By ordinary means, and the angel later blessed the child.
options.note: The conception was expressly not by ordinary means but through the Holy Spirit.

quiz.q: Why is the child to be named Jesus?

options.text: Because He will save His people from their sins, as the name the LORD saves declares.
options.note: The angel ties the name directly to His saving mission in verse 21.

options.text: Because He will be a great teacher and leader of Israel.
options.note: He is teacher and King, but the angel names His mission specifically as saving from sins.

options.text: Because it was a common family name to be passed down.
options.note: The name is chosen by God for its meaning, not merely as a family custom.

options.text: Because He will free Israel from Roman rule.
options.note: The salvation named is from sins, not from political oppression.

quiz.q: What does the name Immanuel mean, and why does Matthew stress it?

options.text: God with us; it declares that in Jesus, God Himself has come to dwell among His people.
options.note: Matthew translates it and frames his Gospel with it, ending on I am with you always.

options.text: God saves us; it points to the rescue Jesus brings.
options.note: That is the meaning of Jesus, not Immanuel; Immanuel means God with us.

options.text: God is powerful; it emphasizes divine might over enemies.
options.note: The name speaks of God's presence with us, not primarily His power over foes.

options.text: God is far above; it stresses His distance and holiness.
options.note: The point is the opposite: God is with us, near, not distant.

quiz.q: How does Joseph respond to the angel's revelation?

options.text: He obeys, taking Mary as his wife and naming the child Jesus.
options.note: Verses 24-25 show his full, obedient response to God's word.

options.text: He believes but delays acting until the child is born.
options.note: He did act at once on waking; he simply had no union with her until the birth.

options.text: He obeys reluctantly, still planning a quiet divorce.
options.note: He abandoned the divorce plan and embraced Mary as his wife.

options.text: He refuses and sends Mary away as first intended.
options.note: The opposite: he obeyed the angel and took Mary as his wife.

quiz.q: What do the two names Jesus and Immanuel together teach about the child?

options.text: That God has come near in the flesh, and He has come to save His people from their sins.
options.note: Immanuel names His presence, Jesus names His mission; together they sum up the Gospel.

options.text: That He is a righteous man specially blessed by God.
options.note: He is more than a blessed man; the names declare Him God with us and the Savior.

options.text: That He is a prophet sent to announce God's coming kingdom.
options.note: He is more than a prophet who announces God; He is God with us who saves.

options.text: That He is only a symbol of God's presence, not truly divine.
options.note: Immanuel means God actually with us; the conception by the Spirit marks true deity.

questions: Joseph was a righteous man whose righteousness bent toward mercy. Where might God be calling you to hold both truth and compassion in a difficult situation?
The angel told Joseph not to be afraid to take Mary as his wife. What fear is God calling you to face in obedience, trusting His word over your own understanding?
Jesus means the LORD saves, and He saves His people from their sins. How does naming your deepest need as sin, rather than mere circumstance, change what you look to Jesus for?
Immanuel means God with us. In what part of your life this week do you most need to remember that God is not distant but near?
Joseph quietly obeyed at real cost, and God accomplished salvation through his faithfulness. Where is God inviting you to trust that your ordinary obedience matters in His larger purposes?

translationNotes.note: Jesus renders the Hebrew Yeshua, the LORD saves; the BSB footnote makes the wordplay explicit, and the angel builds the mission on the meaning of the name.
The quotation is Isaiah 7:14. Matthew follows the Greek reading virgin, parthenos, and adds his own translation of Immanuel as God with us.
Had no union with her renders a Hebrew idiom, literally he did not know her, describing that the marriage was not consummated until after Jesus was born.
